title: Horns Offense
description: The versatile elbow alignment — two bigs up top, endless entries, screens, and counters from one look.
whatIsIt: Horns is an offensive alignment, not a single play: the ball handler up top, a big at each elbow, and wings in the corners. From this one look, teams can run ball screens either side, elbow entries, flex cuts, flares, DHOs, and Spain PNR — all without changing the formation.

Its popularity comes from optionality. The defense sees the same alignment every time but never knows what's coming: a PNR left, a PNR right, a post entry, or a shooter action. That uncertainty is the offense.
Horns is a favorite of coaches at every level because it is easy to teach (one alignment, clear spots) but hard to scout (many options).
whyItMatters: Most offenses telegraph their intentions by their alignment. Horns hides them — the same set produces ten different attacks. For a team, that means less to memorize and more to choose from; for a defense, it means guessing on every possession.

howTo.title: Set the exact spots
howTo.detail: Ball up top, bigs on the elbows (free-throw line extended), wings deep in the corners. Precision matters — sloppy Horns is just a crowd.

howTo.title: Pick your entry
howTo.detail: The simplest entries: ball screen from either elbow, elbow catch and handoff, or a wing entry into flex action. Call the entry, not the whole play.

howTo.title: Use both bigs
howTo.detail: The non-screening big is the secret weapon: re-screen, dive, pop, or flash to the high post. One-big Horns is just a PNR.

howTo.title: Flow to the second side
howTo.detail: If the first action is covered, swing the ball and attack from the other elbow. The defense shifted; punish the new gap.

howTo.title: Keep the corners filled
howTo.detail: Wings stay home until the action commits. Their shooting gravity is what keeps the paint open for everything else.

coachingPoints: Teach the alignment before any plays — players must know their spots cold.
Install one entry per week; Horns with five half-learned options is worse than one mastered.
Let the point guard choose the side — called sides become predictable fast.
Bigs need screening, popping, and short-roll skills; Horns asks a lot of them.
commonMistakes: Bigs setting up too low or too wide, destroying the elbow geometry.
Running the same entry every time — the alignment's power is its variety.
Wings drifting in early and letting help defenders clog the paint.
gameSituations: ATO plays and late-game, when one alignment with many options is ideal.
Teams with two skilled bigs who can screen, pop, and decide.
Against switching defenses, where the second big punishes every switch.
